plan.title: Slow down to catch up
plan.businessGoal: Give every new team member of Aster Orbital Services (fictional client), whatever their background, the intuition behind a rendezvous before they join a satellite-servicing mission: braking to catch up, then pushing back at the same point.

audience.role: New team members of a satellite-servicing company: operators, technicians and support staff
audience.notes: No physics needed: speed, distance and time are enough. Most expect that pushing towards a target brings them closer.

sources.title: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th edition, chapters 2, 6 and 7 (circular orbits, phasing manoeuvres, relative motion)
Fehse, Automated Rendezvous and Docking of Spacecraft, Cambridge University Press, 2003, chapter 3 (phasing and relative trajectories)
NASA, Gemini program mission reports: Gemini 4 (June 1965) and Gemini 6A/7 (December 1965)
AOS-FD-07, Aster Orbital Services flight dynamics handbook: phasing rules of thumb

objectives.statement: Predict whether pushing forwards or backwards brings a spacecraft closer to a satellite ahead of it on the same orbit, and say why.
objectives.criterion: Correct prediction on a rendezvous situation

objectives.statement: Size the first burn of a rendezvous with the rule of thumb: at 500 km, each m/s of braking gains about 17 km per lap.
objectives.criterion: Burn within 5 % of the expected value

objectives.statement: Plan a two-burn rendezvous that meets a distance, time and fuel requirement, and check it on a simulated orbit.

items.title: Slow down to catch up
items.description: The situation: a satellite 50 km ahead on the same orbit, and the question of how to catch it. The hook: in 1965, Gemini 4 pushed towards its target and lost it; Gemini 6A caught Gemini 7 from a lower, faster orbit.

lockedTexts.text: In 1965, the crew of Gemini 4 pushed towards their target. It drifted further away with every push. Six months later, Gemini 6A flew below its target, on a faster orbit, and caught Gemini 7.

items.title: Lower is faster
items.description: Three orbits to scale, from the Space Station to geostationary satellites, shown one by one as the learner selects them: the closer to the Earth, the shorter the lap, and why.

lockedTexts.text: Closer to the Earth, gravity pulls harder: you have to fly faster to stay up, and each lap is shorter.

items.title: The first push
items.description: Prediction before the explanation, unscored: the satellite is 50 km ahead; push forwards, backwards or down? A short feedback on each choice.

items.title: Brake to move ahead
items.description: Once the learner has chosen, what braking does, drawn on the figure: the far side of the orbit dips, the lap gets shorter, the spacecraft gains on the satellite; a push forwards at the same point stops the drift.

lockedTexts.text:
1. You brake: the far side of your orbit dips.
2. Lower is faster: your lap gets shorter.
3. Back at 1, you are closer to the satellite. Push forwards just as hard, and you stop drifting.

items.title: Catch the satellite
items.description: 3D lab of a spacecraft and a satellite on a 500 km orbit, with the rule of thumb beside it: at 500 km, each m/s of braking gains about 17 km per lap. Three rendezvous in a row, each with one instruction and only the controls it needs: catch a satellite 51 km ahead in one lap (the burn alone); the same gap with 2.5 m/s of fuel, in up to three laps (the laps and the fuel appear); let a satellite 34 km behind catch up within two laps. The lab burns back at the same point. Scored.

lockedTexts.text: At 500 km up, each m/s of braking gains about **17 km per lap**.

questions.stem: The satellite is **85 km ahead**, 500 km up. You take **two laps** to catch it. How hard do you brake, in m/s?

feedback.correct: Right: $\dfrac{85}{17 \times 2} = 2.5$ m/s. Two laps later, push forwards 2.5 m/s and you stop drifting.
feedback.incorrect: Each m/s gains about 17 km per lap: divide the gap by 17, then by the number of laps.

misconceptions.feedback: That catches 85 km in one lap. Over two laps, half the burn is enough.
That is the distance to gain on each lap, in km. Divide it by 17 to get m/s.

questions.stem: Two laps later, you are back where you braked, **300 m behind** the satellite. What now?

options.text: Push forwards as hard as you braked
options.feedback: Right: you are back on the satellite's orbit, and you stay 300 m behind it, ready for the final approach.
Your laps are still shorter: one lap later, you would be about 40 km ahead.
Your orbit would dip further, and you would shoot past the satellite.
